C
Confirm the diagnosis of MSF by rickettsial isolation, serology, immunologic detection of rickettsiae in tissue, or polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplification of rickettsial DNA. C
Treat all patients with MSF, including the elderly, children, and pregnant women, with doxycycline. B
Early diagnosis and treatment of MSF is paramount given its high mortality. C
When visiting MSF-endemic areas, avoid close contact with domestic and stray dogs, use tick repellent, and wear protective clothing, preferably impregnated with permethrin or another pyrethroid. C

background.definition: Mediterranean spotted fever (MSF), also known as Boutonneuse fever, is a tick-borne illness caused by Rickettsia conorii, a bacterium transmitted to humans by the dog tick Rhipicephalus sanguineus commonly found in domestic and stray dogs.

list.listitem: MSF is uncommon in the United States; less than 50 imported cases have been clinically and serologically identified by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). This may be attributed to the non-reportability of the disease as well as inadequate recognition of the disease. Figure 1 shows the distribution of MSF around the world.

R. conorii infection occurs in countries and regions adjacent to the Mediterranean Sea, as well as in sub-Saharan Africa, Greece, India, areas around the Black Sea such as Turkey, Bulgaria, and Ukraine, and in Croatia bordering the Adriatic Sea. Sporadic cases have been described in non-endemic regions either in travelers or in patients who had contact with dogs infected from endemic areas.
MSF has a cyclical variation in incidence, with a peak occurring in the summer months from July to September.
Urban populations are as affected as rural populations.

MSF incidence may increase with higher temperatures, lower rainfall, and a decrease in the number of days of frost during the preceding year. This higher incidence during warmer months may be related to an increase in the aggressiveness and propensity of R. sanguineus ticks to bite humans.

In Portugal during the past decade, the number of annual hospitalizations increased from fewer than 200 cases to more than 400 cases. In Oran, Algeria, a peak in MSF incidence was noted in 2005, with 202 cases. This compares with the previous 9 years, where the mean incidence was 132 patients. In Bulgaria, from the beginning of the 1960s, MSF cases decreased sharply but then completely disappeared in the 1970s. However, in 1995 a large increase in MSF disease (236 cases) was noted, reaching 716 cases in 1997. The number of places in Bulgaria where MSF was registered also increased annually.

Since 2005, in addition to 14 European countries, R. conorii was detected in Serbia, Romania, Slovakia, and Malta by serological methods. The seroprevalences of R. conorii infection were 3.9% in Italy, 4.4% in the Canary Islands, 8.7% to 11.2% in Spain, and up to 23% in the Serbian mountain areas. The discrepancy between seroprevalence and incidence rates suggests that some infections may be subclinical or less severe and therefore go undiagnosed.
Currently, MSF seems to be in its second emergence since its discovery.
MSF is more common in men.

With increased travel to endemic areas, more imported cases of MSF are described in travelers returning to the United States and northern Europe from Mediterranean regions. Traveling dogs may carry R. conorii-infected ticks to non-endemic areas.

Physicians who practice in areas far removed from the site of primary infection may face returning travelers with unusual or unfamiliar clinical illnesses that are due to spotted fever group rickettsiae.
Rhipicephalus sanguineus, (Figure 2) the brown dog tick (kennel tick, pantropical dog tick), is the main tick vector and reservoir for R. conorii in Europe and North Africa.
R. sanguineus probably has the most widespread distribution of all ixodid ticks.
Its distribution is confined to localities that have domestic dogs and human dwelling or man-made structures.
Although R. sanguineus adapts well to urban environments, it is relatively host-specific and rarely feeds on people unless its preferred host (the dog) is not available.

Rickettsia conorii, (Figure 3) an obligate intracellular gram-negative bacterium, when transmitted to a susceptible human host, multiplies in endothelial cells of small to medium vessels, causing vasculitis that is responsible for the clinical and laboratory abnormalities that occur.

Proliferation of rickettsiae at the site of the tick bite results in focal epidermal and dermal necrosis called “tache noire” (“black stain”). Rickettsiae then spread via lymphatic vessels to the regional lymph nodes and via the bloodstream to skin, brain, lungs, heart, liver, spleen, and kidneys.

The pathogen invades and proliferates in the endothelial cells of small vessels, destroying them and spreading the infection to the endothelia of the vascular tree. The damage of the endothelium and the subsequent endothelial dysfunction is followed by the activation of acute phase responses. This results in changes in the coagulation and in the cytokine network, together with a transient immune dysregulation characterized by the reduction in peripheral CD4+ T lymphocytes.
After an incubation period of approximately 6 days (1-16 days), the onset of MSF is abrupt.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Classic risk factors for severe or malignant forms of MSF involving 2 or more organ systems include advanced age, immunocompromised status, diabetes, cardiac insufficiency, chronic alcoholism, respiratory insufficiency, glucose-6-phosphate-dehydrogenase deficiency, prior prescription of an inappropriate antibiotic, and delayed treatment.
In Spain, diabetes mellitus, alcohol dependence syndrome, and chronic liver disease are highly associated with risk of hospitalization (10.8%, 2.4%, and 2.8% hospitalization, respectively).

Risk factors for mortality in MSF patients are shown in Table 1. Risk factors for death include encephalitis with brain edema, acute respiratory distress syndrome and non-cardiogenic lung swelling, gastrointestinal bleeding, hemorrhagic-necrotizing pancreatitis, and acute renal failure. Laboratory factors associated with fatality include leukocytosis with marked shift to the left, very high serum urea and creatinine levels, low levels of fibrinogen and prolongation of thrombin time, and serious acid-base balance disturbance.

list.listitem: When visiting MSF-endemic areas, avoid close contact with domestic and stray dogs and wear protective clothing, preferably impregnated with permethrin or another pyrethroid. C
Use tick repellents (eg DEET) on skin and reapply frequently given their short duration of effect (approximately 1 to 2 hours per application). C
Consider wearing long-lasting permethrin-impregnated clothing that allows clothing to retain insecticidal activity for over 70 washes, as this reduces the incidence of tick bites. C
During travel, perform daily self-checks and immediately remove any ticks found. C
No vaccine currently exists for MSF.

Suspect MSF in travelers returning from endemic areas who present within two weeks of exposure with abrupt onset fever, headache, fatigue, myalgias, arthralgias, maculopapular or petechial rash of the palms and soles, and/or an eschar at the tick bite site known as the pathognomonic “tache noir”. C
Confirm the diagnosis of MSF by rickettsial isolation, serology, immunologic detection of rickettsiae in tissue, or PCR amplification of rickettsial DNA. C

Serological tests are generally preferred given their speed and ubiquity. Consider quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) on cutaneous swabs or skin biopsy specimen given its high accuracy in patients where the diagnosis remains uncertain. C
Prior to initiating treatment, perform a skin biopsy of the inoculation eschar given the high concentration of rickettsiae in this clinical sample. C

list.listitem: The duration of illness is typically 12 to 20 days.

Patients usually present with high fever >39 °C (94%-100%), flu-like symptoms including headache, chills, and arthromyalgias (78%), a black eschar (Figure 4) at the tick bite site known as the pathognomonic “tache noir” (53%-77%), and a rash spreading to the palms and soles (87% to 96%) that is either maculopapular (94%) or petechial (6%).
The rash typically follows the fever within 2 to 3 days, although rarely it is delayed until the fifth day.
Gastrointestinal symptoms are present in approximately 30% of patients.

In patients with persistent fever, lasting for 7 days or more, in or traveling from endemic tropical areas, ricketsiossis accounts for a substantial portion of cases (2.3%). Elevated level of alanine transaminase is a moderate predictor of rickettsiosis in these cases, but the usefulness of this feature in clinical practice is questionable due to its nonspecifity and the presence of elevations in other ubiquitous tropical infections.

In recent years, atypical and serious life-threatening presentations of MSF have been reported, also known as malignant forms of MSF. These include presentations with cardiac symptoms (ectasia of the coronary arteries, myocarditis, and atrial fibrillation), ocular symptoms (uveitis, retinopathy, and retinal vasculitis), neurological symptoms (cerebral infarct, meningoencephalitis, sensorineural hearing loss, acute quadriplegia secondary to axonal polyneuropathy, motor and sensory polyneuritis, and peripheral facial nerve palsy), pancreatitis, splenic rupture, acute renal failure, vasculitis, and the presence of hemophagocytic syndrome.
Additionally, patients may develop sepsis from ricketssial infection.
Consider obtaining a CBC with differential, a complete metabolic panel, PT/INR, PTT, fibrinogen, c-reactive protein (CRP), creatine kinase, and a urinalysis.

Laboratory abnormalities can include anemia, leukopenia, leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, prothrombin time >13 seconds, partial thromboplastin time >35 seconds, hyperglycemia, elevated serum creatinine, hyponatremia, hypokalemia, elevated total bilirubin level, and C-reactive protein >0.5 mg/dL. Other abnormalities can include elevated serum levels of urea, alanine transaminase, aspartate transaminase, γ-glutamyl transferase, alkaline phosphatase, and creatinine kinase.
Culture remains extremely difficult for rickettsiae, and confirmatory diagnosis mainly relies on serology and polymerase chain reaction (PCR).
Isolation methods require specialized laboratory facilities.
During the first few days of the disease, when antibodies are not detectable, diagnosis should be based on the detection of the rickettsiae in clinical samples, if possible.
Serologic tests include the Weil Felix (WF) agglutination test, a microimmunofluorescent (MIF) antibody test, an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), and western blot immunoassay.
Immunoassay methods detect convalescent IgM and IgG antibodies 10 to 14 days after the onset of illness, but are usually not useful in the initial clinical management of patients with acute illness.
Biopsies of skin rash, eschar, or other tissues can be useful in the diagnosis. Direct immunofluorescence of cutaneous biopsy specimen can be diagnostic during the acute phase of the disease.

PCR amplification from blood, skin biopsy samples, skin surface swabs, and other tissues can be performed to detect rickettsial DNA and differentiate Rickettsia conorii from other rickettsial species.

Consider MSF in patients with spiking fever, fatigue, myalgias, arthralgias, and/or headache with onset of diffuse rash spreading to the palms and soles 2 to 3 days following the onset of fever. The “tache noir” is a pathognomonic eschar at the site of tick envenomation and rickettsial inoculation.
In a patient presenting with typical symptoms, ask about their travel history and tick exposure or bites.
Obtain acute and convalescent serological confirmatory testing. Additionally, obtain serum, surface swab, or skin biopsy to send for qPCR and culture if possible.
Consider contacting the CDC for reporting and assistance.
Notify the local health department.
Provide early empiric antibiotic therapy to patients with suspected MSF while waiting for confirmation of diagnosis. Doxycycline (200 mg/day) remains the preferred treatment for MSF. B
Although tetracyclines are contraindicated for general use in children younger than 8 years, doxycycline remains the preferred treatment for children who have MSF, including young children. B

Josamycine (50 mg/kg per day; not available in the US) has been used successfully to treat MSF. It can be used when available at a dose of 3 g per day for 7 days in pregnant women who have MSF and at 100 mg/kg per day for 5 days in children less than age 8, or patients with tetracycline allergy. Clarithromycin or azithromycin are also safe alternative agents for pregnant women and children less than 8 years of age. B
Macrolides, fluoroquinolones, and chloramphenicol are reasonable alternatives if doxycycline or josamycine are not available or are contraindicated. B
Doxycycline is a pregnancy risk category D.
shows first-line drugs and duration of therapy for MSF.

Single-day doxycycline therapy may be an effective and well-tolerated treatment for MSF, including in elderly patients and severe cases. In a prospective cohort study of cases with confirmed MSF treated with a single-day doxycycline regimen in a teaching hospital from 1990 to 2015, patients received 2 oral doses of 200 mg of doxycycline for one day. The outcomes evaluated were the time interval between the start of treatment and apyrexia, the time interval between the start of treatment and disappearance of other symptoms, and the adverse reactions to treatment and death. All patients treated with single-day therapy recovered uneventfully, including those greater than age 65 and those with severe cases.
Because the differential diagnosis for MSF includes many rare diseases, consultation with a dermatologist and an infectious disease specialist should be considered.

Strongly consider inpatient hospitalization in the elderly, children, pregnant women, immunocompromised, patients at risk of severe MSF, and those patients with clinical or laboratory features of severe/malignant MSF involving two or more organ systems.
It is an uncommon, but possible, cause of sepsis syndrome. Patients may require intensive care if they manifest multi-organ involvement.
Hospitalize if there is any suspicion by the physician that the patient may not take prescribed oral antibiotics.

MSF is at least as severe as Rocky Mountain spotted fever, with a mortality rate as high as 32%, which was reported in Portugal in 1997. B A mortality rate of 54% has been reported in hospitalized patients with neurological manifestations and multi-organ involvement. B
Defervescence and clinical improvement usually occur within 48 hours of therapy. C
Patients usually recover within 10 days without any sequelae. C
Prognosis significantly worsens in those individuals with severe or malignant MSF. Patients can be risk stratified for progression to severe MSF by a well-defined list of risk factors (see ). B
The elderly are at higher risk of developing severe or malignant forms of MSF.

Gastrointestinal symptoms, impaired consciousness, lung infiltrate, edema, acute hearing loss, raises alanine transaminase, hyponatremia, and thrombocytopenia ocur more frequently in elderly patients. Arthromyalgias occur less frequently.
Single-day doxycycline therapy is a well tolerated and effective treatmennt.
Doxycycline or josamycine are first-line antibiotic choices in pregnant women. Treatment duration is 7 to 10 days.
Clarithromycin or azithromycin are valid alternative therapies to tetracyclines or chloramphenicol, especially for children of less than 8 years of age.
Cervical adenopathy is more frequent in children, occurring in 33% to 74% of cases.
Headache is less frequent in children.
Gastrointestinal symptoms are more likely to occur in children.

In an Italian study of 415 children with MSF, fever, rash, and eschar were present in 93%, 95%, and 63% of cases, respectively, and 5% of children presented with atypical exanthema (petechial, purpuric, papulovesicular, and vesicular). Multiple eschars and clusters of MSF cases have been reported, which are novel findings for MSF because the probability of being bitten simultaneously by several infected Rhipicephalus sanguineus ticks is considered rare.
Children are more likely to experience mild forms of illness. While there are isolated cases of severe and malignant forms, children typically do not suffer the fatal complications seen in adults.
